questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The selective medium for isolating Neisseria gonorrhoeae is:
questions.concept: Thayer-Martin is chocolate agar with vancomycin, colistin and nystatin to suppress commensals. Neisseria are oxidase-positive Gram-negative diplococci; gonococcus ferments only glucose, meningococcus glucose and maltose.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci within neutrophils in a urethral smear from a symptomatic man indicate:
options: Gonorrhoea, for which the smear is highly sensitive and specific
questions.concept: In symptomatic male urethritis the Gram-stained smear is diagnostic, but sensitivity is poor in women and at extragenital sites, where culture or nucleic acid amplification is required.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Recurrent Neisseria infections should prompt investigation for deficiency of:
options: Terminal complement components C5 to C9
questions.concept: The membrane attack complex is required to lyse Neisseria, so terminal complement deficiency causes recurrent meningococcal disease, often with unusual serogroups and a paradoxically milder course.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Chemoprophylaxis of close contacts of a meningococcal meningitis case is with:
questions.concept: Prophylaxis eradicates nasopharyngeal carriage, which penicillin does not achieve despite treating invasive disease. It should be given within 24 hours to household and other close contacts.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Haemophilus influenzae requires which growth factors?
questions.concept: Both factors are supplied by chocolate agar where heat lyses red cells. Satellitism around Staphylococcus colonies on blood agar, which release V factor, is a classic identifying feature.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Hib vaccine protects against invasive disease because it is:
options: A polysaccharide-protein conjugate immunogenic in infants
questions.concept: Plain polysaccharide vaccines are poorly immunogenic under 2 years as they are T-independent antigens; conjugation to a carrier protein recruits T-cell help, giving memory and herd protection in infancy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Bordetella pertussis is best isolated on:
questions.concept: Bordet-Gengou glycerol-potato-blood agar with added penicillin is used, giving mercury-drop colonies. Nasopharyngeal aspirate PCR is now the most sensitive method, as culture yield falls after the catarrhal stage.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The most infectious stage of whooping cough is:
options: The catarrhal stage, before the characteristic cough appears
questions.concept: Infectivity is highest before diagnosis is clinically obvious, which is why contact prophylaxis with a macrolide and high vaccine coverage matter more than treating the established paroxysmal stage.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Brucellosis is diagnosed serologically by:
options: Standard tube agglutination test, with a rising or high titre
questions.concept: The standard agglutination test with titres of 1 in 160 or above supports diagnosis; blood culture on biphasic Castaneda medium is definitive but slow and hazardous to laboratory staff.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Brucellosis in humans is most often acquired from:
options: Unpasteurised milk and milk products, or occupational animal contact
questions.concept: Brucella melitensis from goats and sheep causes the most severe human disease. Veterinarians, abattoir workers and laboratory staff are occupationally at risk, and treatment requires prolonged combination therapy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Rickettsiae are transmitted to humans principally by:
options: Arthropod vectors such as ticks, mites, lice and fleas
questions.concept: All rickettsial infections except Q fever are arthropod-borne obligate intracellular organisms. Q fever from Coxiella burnetii is acquired by inhaling aerosols from infected animal birth products.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Epidemic typhus is caused by and transmitted by:
options: Rickettsia prowazekii transmitted by the human body louse
questions.concept: Louse-borne epidemic typhus occurs in overcrowding and poor hygiene during war and famine. Brill-Zinsser disease is its late recrudescence, and rickettsiae are excreted in louse faeces rubbed into bite wounds.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A to C cause:
options: Trachoma, a leading infectious cause of blindness
questions.concept: Serotypes A to C cause trachoma with follicular conjunctivitis, pannus, Herbert pits and cicatricial entropion with trichiasis; D to K cause genital infection and inclusion conjunctivitis; L1 to L3 cause LGV.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The WHO SAFE strategy for trachoma elimination comprises:
options: Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness and Environmental improvement
questions.concept: Lid surgery for trichiasis, mass azithromycin, facial cleanliness to interrupt fly-borne transmission and environmental improvement including latrines and water form the elimination strategy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The commonest cause of non-gonococcal urethritis is:
options: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D to K
questions.concept: Chlamydial urethritis is often asymptomatic, causing pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy in women and reactive arthritis in HLA-B27 individuals. Doxycycline or azithromycin is used.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Mycoplasma differs from all other bacteria in:
options: Lacking a cell wall, making it inherently resistant to beta-lactams
questions.concept: Absence of peptidoglycan means penicillins and cephalosporins are useless, so macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones are used. Mycoplasma is the smallest free-living organism, giving fried-egg colonies on PPLO agar.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection may be associated with:
options: Cold agglutinin haemolysis and erythema multiforme
questions.concept: Anti-I cold agglutinins cause haemolysis, and extrapulmonary manifestations include erythema multiforme, bullous myringitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome and arthritis. Radiographic changes exceed the clinical findings.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Q fever is distinctive among rickettsial diseases because it:
options: Is acquired by inhalation, has no rash, and may cause culture-negative endocarditis
questions.concept: Coxiella burnetii is highly infectious by aerosol, causing pneumonia and hepatitis without the rash typical of other rickettsioses, and chronic infection presents as culture-negative endocarditis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Lymphogranuloma venereum characteristically shows:
options: A transient painless ulcer followed by painful matted inguinal nodes with a groove sign
questions.concept: Buboes above and below the inguinal ligament are separated by the ligament producing the groove sign, and may rupture forming sinuses. Doxycycline for 21 days is the treatment.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The drug of choice for all rickettsial infections is:
questions.concept: Doxycycline produces defervescence within 48 hours, and this therapeutic response is itself diagnostically useful. Azithromycin is used in pregnancy and young children; beta-lactams are ineffective.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: The immunoglobulin present in highest concentration in serum is:
questions.concept: IgG constitutes about 75% of serum immunoglobulin, is the only class crossing the placenta giving passive neonatal immunity, and predominates in the secondary response. IgA predominates in secretions and IgM in the primary response.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: The first antibody produced in a primary immune response is:
options: IgM, a pentamer and the most efficient complement activator
questions.concept: IgM appears first and its pentameric structure makes it the best agglutinator and complement fixer. Detecting specific IgM therefore indicates recent or acute infection, as in dengue or hepatitis A.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in:
questions.concept: Live organisms may replicate uncontrollably in immunodeficiency and pose a theoretical fetal risk. BCG, OPV, measles, mumps, rubella, varicella and yellow fever are live; mild illness is not a contraindication.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: Passive immunisation with immunoglobulin provides:
options: Immediate but temporary protection without immunological memory
questions.concept: Preformed antibody acts at once but wanes over weeks, and is used post-exposure for rabies, tetanus, hepatitis B and diphtheria alongside active immunisation, which provides durable memory but takes time.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: The cold chain is required for vaccines because:
options: Heat and, for some vaccines, freezing destroy potency
questions.concept: OPV and measles are the most heat-sensitive, while DPT, hepatitis B and TT are damaged by freezing and must never be frozen - a common field error detected by the shake test.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated individuals by:
options: Reducing the number of susceptible hosts so transmission chains break
Eliminating the pathogen from the environment
questions.concept: Herd immunity works only for person-to-person transmitted infections; it does not apply to tetanus, which is acquired from the environment, so every individual must be immunised.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: The complement pathway activated directly by antigen-antibody complexes is:
questions.concept: IgM or IgG immune complexes bind C1q initiating the classical pathway; the alternative pathway is activated directly by microbial surfaces and the lectin pathway by mannose-binding lectin, all converging on C3.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: ELISA detects antigen or antibody using:
options: An enzyme-linked conjugate producing a measurable colour change
questions.concept: ELISA is sensitive, quantifiable and suited to large-scale screening as in HIV and hepatitis testing. Western blot, detecting antibodies to separated proteins, was traditionally the confirmatory test.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: Natural killer cells differ from cytotoxic T cells in that they:
options: Kill without prior sensitisation and are inhibited by MHC class I
questions.concept: NK cells detect missing self - loss of MHC class I on virus-infected or tumour cells - and also kill via antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity through CD16, bridging innate and adaptive immunity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Innate & adaptive immunity, antigen-antibody reactions, vaccines
questions.stem: BCG is given intradermally rather than subcutaneously because:
options: Deeper injection causes abscess formation and ulceration
questions.concept: Intradermal injection over the left deltoid insertion produces a wheal, then a papule, pustule and healed scar over 6 to 12 weeks. Subcutaneous injection causes cold abscess and axillary lymphadenitis.
